title: Interoception, proprioception and the vestibular system in everyday life
lede: Hunger, thirst, pain, the need to use the toilet, body position and balance depend on different systems. There is no single ‘sensory difficulty’ that explains everything.

p: Use reminders for water, food and toilet breaks; wear clothing appropriate for the temperature even if the sensation arrives late; use visual cues; take movement breaks; and use balance supports when recommended by a professional.
Not noticing thirst, pain or the need to use the toilet can have physical consequences. A functional reminder is an adjustment, not training to ‘feel correctly’.

If there is dizziness, falling, loss of balance, unrecognised pain or new changes, look for medical causes. Vestibular or proprioceptive exercises should not be prescribed generically without a specific need.

title: Emotional regulation, rumination, rejection, guilt and perfectionism
lede: Regulating an emotion does not mean no longer feeling it. The everyday goal is to recognise what is happening, reduce harm and regain the ability to make decisions.

p: Lower demands, use less language, let the person move away from the situation if they want to, postpone important decisions and avoid demanding a complete explanation at the height of the emotion.

Review what happened beforehand, what interpretation arose and what consequences followed. With rumination or perfectionism, limiting endless review by using ‘good enough’ criteria may be more useful than seeking complete certainty.

If guilt, fear of rejection, anger, rumination or shame persistently restrict everyday life, occur alongside self-harm or suicide risk, or appear with depression, OCD or anxiety, a specific assessment is needed.

title: Sleep: what to observe and where to start
lede: Poor sleep is not one single problem. A person may struggle to fall asleep, stay asleep, wake too early or sleep for enough hours without feeling rested. The cause and the support depend on the pattern.

p: Keep a record for one or two weeks: bedtime, how long it takes to fall asleep, awakenings, final waking time, naps, medication, caffeine, pain, activity and how the person functions the next day. This helps distinguish an irregular schedule from a persistent problem.

Reasonably regular times, a clear contrast between day and night, daylight and activity during the day, a transition routine before bed, and reducing stimuli that maintain alertness. For chronic insomnia, specific behavioural sleep treatment has stronger evidence than relying only on ‘sleep hygiene’.

The Spanish consensus published in 2026 recommends starting with assessment, a sleep diary and personalised non-pharmacological measures. Medication is a professional decision and requires follow-up and reassessment; a web entry should not turn doses from a clinical consensus into self-medication instructions.

title: Food, explained through the senses
lede: Texture, smell, temperature, the sound of chewing, foods touching or being mixed, and predictability can completely change the experience of eating. Sensory-based selective eating is not automatically the same as ARFID or another eating disorder.

p: Rejecting mixed or lumpy textures; preferring specific brands, shapes or temperatures; rejecting food because of its smell before tasting it; difficulty eating in unfamiliar places; and needing foods not to touch.

First record what is already eaten; keep safe foods available; make one change at a time; present the new food alongside a familiar one; avoid deception or hidden mixing; and separate the nutritional goal from the goal of ‘eating like everyone else’.

sections.h: When to move to the clinical entry
p: If there is weight loss or altered growth, signs of deficiency, dependence on supplements or enteral feeding, binge eating, compensatory behaviours, consumption of non-food substances or severe interference with everyday life, ARFID, eating disorders, pica or other medical causes need to be assessed.

title: Hygiene and self-care
lede: Showering, brushing teeth, cutting nails, caring for hair or changing clothes are sequences involving touch, temperature, smell, balance, time and planning. Support should target the difficult step rather than judging willingness.

sections.h: Find the point where things get stuck
p: Is it difficult to start, tolerate the water, cope with the brush, remember every step, enter the bathroom or finish? Changing everything at once makes it impossible to know what works.

A visual sequence; fragrance-free products; a towel ready beforehand; a timer; an electric or manual toothbrush depending on tolerance; a shower seat if needed; cutting nails in several short sessions; clothes organised into complete outfits; and choosing the time of day when the person has more energy.

Autonomy includes taking part in decisions about one's own body and accepting help when it is needed. Where someone is dependent on support for basic activities of daily living, Ley 39/2006 provides for support within Spain's autonomy and dependency system.

title: Cooking and safety at home
lede: Cooking combines planning, working memory, coordination, heat, knives, smells and time management. A person may be able to prepare some meals safely and need support with others.

sections.h: Design a kitchen that can actually be used
p: Keep frequently used utensils visible, use recipes with numbered steps, gather ingredients before turning on the heat and reduce the number of decisions. No-cook ‘assembly’ meals also count as everyday cooking.

Use visible timers, hobs with automatic shut-off where possible, turn pan handles inward, use suitable oven gloves and have a clear rule about which tasks require another person. If there is epilepsy, fainting, motor difficulty or altered risk judgement, adapt the type of cooking.
Practise one recipe until it becomes familiar before adding another. The goal is food preparation that is safe enough and sustainable, not mastery of complex cooking techniques.

title: Organisation, planning, executive functions and everyday tasks
lede: Knowing what needs to be done does not guarantee being able to start it, put it in order and finish it. Working memory, estimating time, switching between tasks and emotional load can block simple actions.

p: Turn ‘tidy the bedroom’ into observable actions; leave the next item ready; use short lists; keep a ‘pending’ tray; use calendars with only a few categories; and set alarms that say what to do, not simply that ‘an alarm has gone off’.

Reduce the first step until it is doable: open the document, put the clothes next to the washing machine, take out a frying pan. For some people, starting alongside another person — in person or remotely — helps even when each person is doing their own task.
If an organisational system requires maintaining ten apps, colour codes and daily reviews, it can become another task. The best system is the one that still works during a difficult week.

title: Rest, fatigue, masking and recovery
lede: Rest is not only sleep. It can also mean reducing conversation, decisions, light, travel, emotional work or the need to appear fine. Recovery requires a real reduction in demands.

sections.h: Signs that rest is not enough
p: Starting tasks, tolerating noise, speaking, eating, making decisions or maintaining routines that used to be possible becomes increasingly difficult. There is no need to wait for a crisis before reorganising the load.

Periods without interaction, days with fewer transitions, simple meals, automating tasks, working from a less stimulating space where possible, and allowing recovery time after high-demand activities.

The term has a growing research literature but no validated diagnostic criteria. If exhaustion is intense or prolonged, depression, anaemia, pain, sleep, medication and other medical causes also need to be considered; calling everything ‘burnout’ can hide them.
